# Education in Israel
Israel’s education system spans three tiers: primary, middle, and high school, with compulsory education from kindergarten through 12th grade. Schools are categorized into four tracks: state-secular, state-religious, independent religious (Haredi), and Arab, with increasing representation from the Haredi and Arab sectors. The Haredi track largely emphasizes religious studies, leading to low participation in mainstream education and workforce, prompting government initiatives to integrate them better professionally. Arab schools provide education in Arabic, focusing on Arab culture and history but face challenges including underfunding and infrastructure shortages.
Higher education is highly valued culturally, with strong historic roots and significant investment, making Israel one of the OECD leaders in tertiary education attainment. High schools prepare students for the matriculation (Bagrut) exams, which affect military, academic, and employment opportunities. Universities require matriculation and Psychometric Entrance Test scores, with programs subsidized by the government. Israel’s universities rank highly globally, particularly in science and engineering fields. Despite achievements, educational inequalities persist, especially affecting Arab and Haredi communities. Gender disparities exist, with women outperforming men academically but underrepresented in STEM fields. Teacher pay is relatively low leading to strikes, and textbooks have been critiqued for bias issues. The system has also experienced numerous strikes over pay and conditions.

# Education in Sri Lanka
Sri Lanka’s education system is overseen by multiple ministries covering schools, universities, and vocational training. Education history spans over 2300 years, initially based on Buddhist monastic schools (pirivenas) and later influenced by Christian missionary schools during colonial times. Primary and secondary education is structured into five parts: primary, junior secondary, senior secondary, collegiate, and tertiary. Free education was formalized in 1938, with national languages as media of instruction.
The system includes government schools categorized as national, provincial, and pirivenas; private and international schools are also widespread. Tertiary education is competitive and mostly free in public universities with limited access, leading many qualified students to study abroad or in private institutions. Vocational education is coordinated by the Tertiary and Vocational Education Commission with structured qualification levels. Tuition classes are common due to exam competitiveness and have become a significant industry. Education has faced criticism for rigidity and competition, as well as mandatory military-style leadership training for undergraduates, which ended in 2015.

# Education in the Republic of Ireland
Irish education entails compulsory schooling from ages 6 to 16 (or three years of secondary education). The system includes pre-school, primary (Junior and Senior Infants through Sixth Class), and secondary education comprising Junior (3 years), optional Transition Year, and Senior Cycle (2 years) culminating in Junior and Leaving Certificate exams. The curriculum is broad and designed to nurture child development in multiple dimensions with core subject emphasis.
Schools are predominantly under church patronage, especially Roman Catholic, though multidenominational and language immersion (Gaelscoileanna) schools are increasing. Secondary education is delivered through voluntary secondary, community colleges, comprehensive schools, and fee-charging grind schools. Ireland ranks highly in international assessments for reading and math. Special needs education is supported through dedicated laws and assistants. Disadvantaged schools receive targeted support via the DEIS program. Ireland attracts international students to both schools and universities.

text:
# Education in Egypt
Egypt’s education has ancient roots, with institutions like the Bar Ankh and the ancient University of Alexandria. Medieval education centered on institutions like Al-Azhar and the Dar al-Ilm. Modern reforms began under Muhammad Ali in the 19th century, introducing secular and religious dual systems. British occupation caused neglect and restriction of access to education, lifted partially after 1907.
Contemporary education is centralized and free at basic levels, with nine years of compulsory basic education (kindergarten through preparatory). Secondary education splits into general and technical tracks, while higher education includes numerous public and private institutions under centralized governance, though facing quality and resource challenges. Al-Azhar operates a parallel religious school system with significant enrollment. Private tutoring is widespread due to inadequacies in public education. Recent reforms focus on quality, decentralization, and incorporating technology. Challenges include disparities, teacher quality, high unemployment among graduates, and disparities in access.

# Education in Nigeria
Nigeria’s education system includes six years of primary, three years junior secondary, and three years senior secondary education. The Universal Basic Education program guarantees free and compulsory nine years of basic education. Secondary education encompasses Federal Government Colleges (“unity schools”), state-funded, and private/religious schools. Examinations include SSCE/GCE administered by WAEC and NECO. Advanced Level programs (IJMB, JUPEB) provide pathways to university direct entry.
Tertiary education features over 150 universities (federal, state, private), polytechnics, and colleges regulated by the Nigerian Universities Commission. Vocational education and informal apprenticeships remain central but face challenges such as teacher shortages and outdated curricula. Literacy rates are low with regional disparities; ongoing efforts target improving both traditional and digital literacy by 2030. Female education faces barriers from social, cultural, and security issues, with UNICEF-supported programs promoting girls’ education. Rural education suffers from poor infrastructure and understaffing. International schools serve expatriates and elite families.

# Education in Indonesia
Indonesia’s education evolved from Islamic pesantren and colonial Dutch systems that segregated education by social class and ethnicity. The national system, post-independence, recognizes both public secular schools and religious schools, with compulsory 12 years of education divided into primary, junior and senior secondary levels. Kindergarten (PAUD) is optional. Primary school lasts six years; junior and senior secondary three years each, with academic and vocational tracks at higher levels.
The national curriculum emphasizes Pancasila ideology and often employs rote learning. Islamic schools (pesantren, madrasah) vary widely in religious and secular content. Indonesian higher education includes universities, institutes, and polytechnics offering academic, vocational, and professional tracks aligned with the Indonesian National Qualification Framework. Challenges include funding, teacher quality, access disparities, and educational quality, especially in remote areas.

# Education in Taiwan
Taiwan’s education system combines historical influences from Dutch, Qing, Japanese, and Chinese administrations. Twelve years of compulsory education cover elementary to junior high school. Senior high school offers academic and skill-based tracks, with national exams determining university entrance. Universities offer bachelor’s through doctoral degrees and vocational education at junior colleges and institutes of technology.
Education is predominantly in Mandarin, with instruction in native languages and English. Private education, including extensive cram schools, is widespread due to cultural emphasis on academic achievement. Universities have research prominence and international programs. Special education and adult education services exist. Educational reforms emphasize in-service teacher training and integration of technology.

# Education in Armenia
Armenia achieved 100% literacy early and followed Soviet education models until independence, after which curricula emphasized Armenian language and culture. Compulsory and free primary and secondary education spans 12 years, divided into primary, middle, and high school, with examinations determining university eligibility. Public schools dominate, though private schools—following strict accreditation—offer specialized programs.
Higher education includes 26 state universities and numerous private institutions, strong in sciences, technology, and Armenian studies. Armenia engages in European educational frameworks (Lisbon Convention, Bologna Process) and participates in EU mobility programs. Challenges include school absenteeism and dropouts linked to child labor. Technology-based afterschool centers help develop modern skills.

# Education in Iran
Iran has a long history of formal education, evolving through pre-Islamic, Safavid, Qajar eras, and reforms post-1979 revolution emphasizing Islamization and gender segregation. Education is centralized under the Ministry of Education, compulsory from ages 6–14, continuing optionally through secondary and higher education. Students take national exams (“konkur”) for university entrance.
Primary to secondary education involves religious and secular courses, with the Upper Secondary phase divided into theoretical, technical-vocational, and manual branches. Higher education includes numerous public and private universities, mostly state-funded, with a high female student representation in recent decades. The education reform emphasizes modern curricula, entrepreneurship, and hybrid learning post-pandemic. Challenges include teacher shortages, regional disparities, private school cost inflation, and politicization of education.

# Education in Norway
Norway’s education system features compulsory primary (grades 1–7), lower secondary (grades 8–10), and optional upper secondary (grades VG1–VG3). Literacy training dates back millennia, with reforms introducing the folkeskole and later the grunnskole as compulsory education. Primary and lower secondary focus on broad foundational knowledge, while upper secondary offers general and vocational tracks. The “Reform 94” unified various secondary paths.
Teachers hold credentials based on degree levels, with varied roles from preschool teacher to university lecturer. Higher education includes universities, university colleges, and private schools. Special education is integrated within mainstream schools, with support services provided. Grading uses numeric and letter systems. The academic year spans August to June, with vacations and national holidays. Norway boasts high PISA scores in Scandinavia.

# Education in Turkey
Turkey’s education evolved from Ottoman religious and reform schools to a unified secular public system post-1924. Compulsory education is now 12 years (4+4+4 system). Primary (İlköğretim) and secondary (including Anatolian and vocational high schools) are state-controlled, with increasing private and international institutions.
Higher education includes public and foundation universities, admission via national exams, with technical institutions achieving international accreditation. Religious education was removed post-Kemalist reforms, reintroduced gradually, currently mandatory with a mixture of secular and Islamic content and noted controversies such as removal of evolution from curricula.
Foreign languages, mainly English, are taught with increasing attention, alongside minority language offerings. Education emphasizes Turkish nationalism and secularism, with controversies around curriculum bias, particularly denial of Armenian genocide. Private schools are diverse and growing. Significant reforms and political influence shape education, with rising international student penetration.

text:
# Education in Sweden
Sweden offers a comprehensive nine-year compulsory school (grundskola) starting ages six to seven, followed by optional three-year upper secondary school (gymnasium) offering preparatory and vocational programmes. Preschool is widely available and subsidized.
The curriculum mandates 16 compulsory subjects, with grading from year 6 onwards using A-F scale. National tests ensure assessment standardization. Upper secondary offers 18 national programmes with diplomas required for further studies. Higher education follows Bologna Process cycles with bachelor, master, and doctoral degrees and uses several grading systems.
Private independent “free schools” (friskolor) publicly funded constitute over 10% of enrollment, sparking debate over profit motives and standards. Sweden participates actively in international education comparisons, with some performance fluctuations attributed partly to immigrant integration challenges. The education system strongly emphasizes inclusion, anti-discrimination, and lifelong learning.

# Education in France
France has a centralized education system from preschool (maternelle) through university, emphasizing secularism since Jules Ferry’s reforms in the late 19th century. Primary education lasts five years, followed by four years of collège (middle school) and three years of lycée (high school), culminating in the baccalauréat exam.
Higher education divides between public universities and elite grandes écoles, with preparatory classes for selective grandes écoles. Universities offer Licence (bachelor), Master, and Doctorate degrees, aligned with the Bologna Process. The system employs competitive exams and oral assessments (“colles”) and features a tiered teacher recruitment system.
Private schools are either “under contract” following the state curriculum or fully independent with religious instruction. France bans conspicuous religious symbols in schools and promotes a uniform national curriculum, with ongoing debates over identity and integration. Tuition is primarily state-subsidized, keeping higher education fees low.

# Education in Hong Kong
Hong Kong’s education has evolved from traditional village schools and missionary-run institutions under British colonial influence to a mixed system with compulsory primary and secondary education. The system comprises preschool, primary (6 years), junior secondary (3 years), senior secondary (3 years) culminating in the HKDSE exam, and tertiary education.
Instruction shifted largely from English-medium to Chinese (Cantonese and increasingly Putonghua) since the 1990s, with bilingual and international schools prevalent. The government funds public schools; aided, subsidized, and private international schools complement the system. Recent political changes have influenced curriculum content and enrolment patterns.
Higher education includes eight UGC-funded universities recognized internationally, with additional self-financing and private institutions. Adult, special needs, and immigrant education are provided, with ongoing focus on language integration. Private tutoring (“cram schools”) remains popular. Cooperation with Guangdong and AI integration in teaching mark recent developments.

# Education in England
England mandates schooling or education/training from ages 5 to 18, with early years foundation stage followed by four key stages in primary and secondary levels. Education types include state-funded schools (community, academies, free schools, faith schools), grammar (selective), and private schools.
The National Curriculum governs compulsory subjects with standardized assessments (GCSEs, A-levels), and post-16 education includes further education colleges and apprenticeships. Higher education features universities and colleges awarding degrees from certificates to doctorates, with funding through tuition fees and loans.
Inspection by Ofsted ensures standards in schools, while private schools enjoy curricular independence. Home education is legal. England ranks well in literacy and skills assessments and has a stratified but comprehensive education sector with ongoing funding and equality measures.

# Education in Ghana
Ghana’s education evolved from informal oral traditions and apprenticeship to formal missionary and colonial schooling. Post-independence reforms introduced free and compulsory basic education (ages 4–14), divided into kindergarten, primary, and junior high school, followed by senior high school or vocational training.
Tertiary education includes universities and polytechnics, with growing private participation and government policy supporting access and equity. Vocational education remains fragmented, with informal apprenticeship dominant. Literacy rates and enrollment have improved significantly, although disparities persist, especially for females and rural populations.
Ghana integrates ICT in education, faces challenges in infrastructure and teacher quality, and relies on public-private partnerships for delivery. The system emphasizes inclusivity, literacy campaigns, and expanding access at all levels amidst economic and social challenges.
This summary consolidates key aspects of education systems, structures, challenges, historical contexts, and reforms across Israel, Sri Lanka, Ireland, Egypt, Nigeria, Indonesia, Taiwan, Armenia, Iran, Norway, Turkey, Sweden, France, Hong Kong, England, and Ghana.
